dimensions.gloss: How much of the output the machine produced relative to the human, usually as an ordered scale or graded category running from none/human-written to fully AI-generated.
dimensions.note: Folds together output-level scales (Generation facet, AIAS levels), coding schemes for extent (how AI involvement was operationalised), grade-level and institutional permitted-use scales (K-12 framework, levels of GenAI adoption), and contribution-weighting scales (Levels of Contribution, investment) whose values describe the same underlying amount-of-AI/human-labor axis even though the objects being graded differ (a text, a policy, a grade).

dimensions.gloss: The graded requirement level attached to disclosing AI use (e.g. mandatory, recommended, optional), independent of how much AI was actually used.

The broad normative principles and thematic scope bundled under the heading "governance" in a scheme (accountability, disclosure infrastructure, ethics, oversight duties), rather than a single measurable scale.
dimensions.note: These are umbrella/thematic labels naming the same overarching duty-and-principle territory rather than one operationalized axis; grouped on that basis, which is a closer call than most other groups here.

dimensions.gloss: The concrete metadata fields (linkage keys, timestamps, reviewer actions, override reasons) kept to document who did what and when during AI-assisted review.
Who holds decision authority, ongoing control, or ultimate responsibility for AI-assisted work and its outputs.
dimensions.note: 'human involvement' is a bare, context-free variant that could instead belong with the extent-of-AI-involvement scale; placed here because it lacks the graded-scale wording ('level of...') that the extent group's members share. 'Governance and ownership' is included because its content ('who exercises ongoing control... power to revise, suspend, or retire it') is an authority/accountability question, not a principles list.

dimensions.gloss: The type or maturity tier of an institution's overall governance approach to AI (e.g. prohibitionist vs. integration-as-pedagogy; textual-integrity vs. disclosure-based vs. computational-integrity models), as a classification of governance philosophy rather than an amount of permitted AI use.
dimensions.note: Distinguished from extent-of-ai-involvement: these grade the kind of policy stance an institution takes, not how much AI is present in a given work.

dimensions.gloss: How open or opaque a repository's or system's governance process itself is (opaque/partial/full), as opposed to what the governance principles are.
The subject-matter or output-type category in which AI was applied (e.g. immunology, graphical abstracts), used to catalogue where AI shows up rather than how it was used.
An enumeration of the roles/actors to whom disclosure guidance applies (authors, editors, reviewers, publishers; advertisers, influencers, ad-tech intermediaries), i.e. who the rules address.
variants: guidance for authors, editors, reviewers, and publishers

dimensions.canonical_label: Purpose or task of AI use
dimensions.gloss: Why AI was used or what kind of task it performed (linguistic correction, transformation, generation, conceptual support, writing-only scope), as opposed to how much was produced.
variants: guidance limited to the writing process

dimensions.gloss: The technical mechanism used to cryptographically verify or attest to provenance or identity (hardware-rooted/TEE-based attestation, identity-focused attestation, DNS-verified digital signature).
dimensions.note: 'Handtekening' (Dutch for 'signature') describes a DNS-verified cryptographic signature field, functionally the same kind of verification mechanism as the attestation types, so it is included here rather than kept separate.

dimensions.gloss: Whether adverse events and error taxonomies arising from AI use are documented.
Mismatches between who actually contributed and who is credited as author, covering both under-crediting (ghost authorship) and over-crediting (honorary authorship).
The explanation of how and why particular data were used in the work.
variants: how and why the data were used

dimensions.gloss: The stated criteria or test used to decide who qualifies as an author (substantial contribution, drafting, final approval, accountability; or, in a legal register, control, creative input, and expressive intent).
variants: How authorship is determined e.g ., a stated criteria by the contributors and/or the resource
dimensions.note: 'identifiable expressive intent' is a copyright-law variant of the same authorship-eligibility test (control, creative input, expressive intent) rather than the ICMJE-style criteria the other members use; included here as the closest-matching axis, but it is a close call.

dimensions.gloss: Whether and how AI-generated content was checked, corrected, confirmed, or agreed upon by a human before use.
variants: How did you evaluate the AI-generated feedback?
dimensions.note: 'human review confirmation' is an attestation that checking occurred rather than a description of the checking method itself; placed here rather than in the human-oversight-and-accountability group because its content is about confirming a verification action took place.

dimensions.gloss: The process by which the underlying data were produced or created.
variants: information related to the creation of the re- search data

dimensions.gloss: How an endorser obtained the product being featured (e.g. gifted vs. purchased), relevant to sponsorship/conflict disclosure.
variants: how the YouTuber got the product

dimensions.gloss: Usability, workflow-fit, and risk-control considerations documented for the humans who use an AI system.
The specific sub-criteria (formal knowledge representation language, FAIR vocabularies, qualified references to other metadata) under the FAIR 'Interoperable' principle for data/metadata.
variants: I3: Qualified references to other metadata

dimensions.gloss: Compliance with a named external standard (adapted from ICMJE) that bundles disclosure, authorship, human responsibility, review, and no-plagiarism requirements together.
dimensions.note: Kept as its own dimension rather than split across the authorship/verification/attribution groups because the label names one bundled external standard, not a single measurable axis.

dimensions.gloss: Whether the identity of who contributed is deliberately concealed.
Whether research data carries a persistent identifier.

dimensions.canonical_label: Presence of a general AI disclosure statement
dimensions.gloss: Whether a general, top-level statement disclosing AI use exists at all, and whether/how it is made.
variants: if and how this is disclosed
dimensions.note: Merges a research-publishing checklist item (GAMER's 'general declaration') with an advertising-domain item ('if and how this is disclosed') because both record the same bare existence-and-method-of-disclosure question; a cross-domain close call.

dimensions.canonical_label: AI use restrictions by content type
dimensions.gloss: Whether AI-generated visual or data content (images, figures) is permitted, conditionally allowed, or prohibited.
The specific application scenarios (location privacy, likeness provenance, fingerprint-based recovery) for an image-provenance verification technology.

dimensions.canonical_label: Research phase where AI was used
dimensions.gloss: Which stage or section of the research process (literature/information gathering, data interpretation, conclusions, IMRaD structure) AI involvement is attached to, and its effect there.
dimensions.note: 'impact on conclusion' and 'IMRaD traceability requirements' blend phase-location with an assessment of AI's downstream effect, but both still key on which part of the research process is at issue, so they are grouped here as a close call.

dimensions.gloss: How credit for source material is given through defined attribution policy or in-text citation.
The pattern by which an AI-use policy is implemented in practice, as one of several coded dimensions of policy compliance.
Whether inclusivity and representational fairness are addressed as a consideration in AI use or its assessment.
Whether and what kind of label, tag, or warning marks AI-generated or synthetic content for an audience.
Whether the AI's contribution was indispensable (vs. incidental) to the work, drawing on concepts of indispensability and specificity.
Enumerated categories of tasks or roles (e.g. CRediT-style: conceptualization, methodology, data interpretation) used to credit specific contributions to a work.
dimensions.note: 'interpretation of data' is included as one named item in a nine-part authorship-components taxonomy (conception, design, ..., interpretation of data, ...), matching this group's role-taxonomy axis rather than the research-phase-of-AI-use axis.

dimensions.gloss: A taxonomy of deceptive industry practices around evidence (misleading quoting, mimicked scientific critique, evidential landscaping).
A categorical judgment of how directly connected an output is to a given influence (direct, implicit, or no connection).
An escalating tier scheme for the type/depth of influence AI-generated advertising exerts (product mentions through long-term preference shaping).
A description of the type or nature of research data being disclosed.
variants: Information about the type of research data

dimensions.gloss: One named sub-dimension (information access literacy) within a broader multi-part AI-literacy framework.
What data was fed into the AI system, its sensitivity level, and what redactions or protections were applied.
Qualitative coding categories (plagiarism, citation and reference, reasons for not citing) used to analyze citation behavior around AI-generated content.
The degree of proactive initiative a contributor took in helping produce the work.
A criterion for evaluating novelty in the technology, design, or approaches used to create, manage, or use data/software.
variants: Innovation in the technology, design, or approaches employed to create, manage, and use data and/or software

dimensions.gloss: Which training data or external code instances are associated with a given AI output.
Whether institutional, legal, or ethical approval/agreements were obtained and recorded before AI use.
The type of relationship (interprets, summarises, implements, applies to, requires, depends on) between institutional policy documents.
How deeply AI-suggested material was merged into the final work, from unedited copy-paste through light edit and adaptation to deep integration.
dimensions.note: Kept distinct from extent-of-ai-involvement: that axis is about how much of the output AI produced overall, this one is about how thoroughly whatever AI produced was blended into the final text.

dimensions.gloss: A stated commitment to intellectual honesty and personal responsibility for research conduct and data integrity.
variants: Integrity (in medical education and quality of clinical research)

dimensions.gloss: Whether the human retained ownership and control of the ideas, structure, and argument of the work versus ceding them to AI.
How rights, licensing, and IP ownership of AI-generated material are handled or considered.
A named element (Intellectual Quality) of a pre-existing educational quality-assurance framework, cited as context rather than as a disclosure field itself.
Identifying which specific AI tools were used, by name, version, and date accessed.
dimensions.note: Kept separate from purpose-of-AI-use: although the source also asks whether the tool was assistive or generative, its primary content is naming/versioning the tool, a different axis from why it was used.

dimensions.gloss: Whether purposeful intent underlay the AI-assisted act, as one evaluative dimension of creative agency.

dimensions.canonical_label: Modality and interactivity of AI system
dimensions.gloss: The medium (text, audio, video, multimodal) and degree of responsiveness an AI system affords.
Compliance with named IOM guideline-development standards.
Risk-related factors (severity, exploitability, mitigation availability, irreversibility, time-criticality, public benefit of transparency) used to decide how urgently disclosure is warranted.

dimensions.canonical_label: Software activity scope for AI policy
dimensions.gloss: Which activity domain (issues/bugs/security, as distinct from code contributions or communication) an AI-use policy's permission level applies to.
How much detail, and at what granularity or layering, a disclosure statement or documentation practice provides.
variants:
levels of information 
detail that can support readers with different engagement goals 
and AI literacy levels
dimensions.note: 'layered information' and 'iterative documentation' describe a design/practice for varying disclosure depth rather than a single detail value, but both still key on how much/what layer of detail is exposed, so they are grouped here as a close call.

dimensions.gloss: Whether a task design contains a point at which the human must select, reject, or defend a choice without AI mediation.
The legal/court mechanism (judicial notice, gatekeeping) by which AI capability or AI-related evidence is formally recognized or admitted.
The jurisdiction and conditions of use under which a disclosure requirement applies.
A rubric's criteria (collaborative authorship, task complexity, opportunity for creativity) for evaluating whether an educational assessment remains valid given AI use.
Whether a repository or record provides descriptive keywords metadata.
Whether the development of a student's thinking or learning process can be observed, via records of who did what, when, and on what evidence.
Legal disclaimers about the responsibility and liability borne by a registry or repository.
variants: Legal disclaimers about the responsibility and liability borne by the registry or repository

dimensions.canonical_label: Legitimacy of AI use per institutional norms
dimensions.gloss: Whether AI use aligns with institutional rules and professional norms (legitimacy), as distinct from whether it is merely effective.
The level (discourse, article content, article attribution) at which bias arising from AI use is measured.
Whether AI-generated advertising disclosure is covert or overt.
Where a goal falls in a specificity hierarchy (parent goals vs. child goals), unrelated to AI content per se.
A disclosed statement of a tool's non-recommended uses and the limits of its data generalizability.
Whether a repository uses a recognized community standard for representing basic metadata.
